items.explanation: The passage says pleasure fades because attention moves on, novelty wears off and the mind compares the present with a better remembered past, so a flat life is a life that no longer surprises. It does not claim pleasure is immoral, that repetition makes it stronger, or that memory has no role.
options: Because pleasure is immoral and therefore cannot last in a good life
Because attention moves on, novelty wears off, and the mind measures the present against a better remembered past
Because the body becomes physically unable to feel pleasure after the age of thirty
Because pleasure is strongest when it is repeated in exactly the same way every day
Because memory plays no part in how pleasure is experienced
items.passage: Pleasure is famously difficult to sustain. A new house delights for a month, a promotion for a week, a favourite meal for an evening, and then the feeling fades, not because the thing has changed but because we have. Philosophers have long noticed this pattern, and psychologists now give it a name: hedonic adaptation. The mind adjusts to a new level of comfort and then treats it as the baseline, so what once felt like a gain soon feels like nothing at all. The puzzle is why we keep chasing the next gain if we know it will fade. Part of the answer is that pleasure is less a property of things than a property of attention. A first taste surprises us, and surprise is pleasant. A tenth taste is familiar, and familiarity, however comfortable, is not exciting. Novelty is therefore not a luxury added to pleasure; it is close to its engine. Another part is comparison. We do not judge a holiday by how pleasant it was in itself, but by how it compares with the best holiday we remember, and memory, being selective, remembers the peak and forgets the rain. Sustaining pleasure, then, is not a matter of accumulating more of the things that pleased us. It is a matter of managing attention and memory: varying the routine so that surprise can return, paying close attention to ordinary experiences instead of letting them pass unnoticed, and refusing to let a remembered peak become the standard against which every present moment is judged and found wanting. None of this makes pleasure permanent, and the passage does not pretend otherwise. It suggests only that a flat life is often not a life without good things, but a life in which good things have stopped being noticed, and that noticing, unlike acquiring, is a skill that can be practised. Gratitude practices are sometimes proposed as a remedy, and they work, when they work, for the same reason. Writing down three good things each evening does not change the facts of a life, but it changes what the mind notices, and what it remembers. The practice is not magic, and it can feel forced at first, like learning to notice a familiar street after years of walking it without looking. Yet over weeks, the habit of noticing accumulates, and the past begins to look fuller, not because more good things happened but because more of them were recorded. The point is not to pretend that hardship does not exist, but to ensure that the record of a life is not written only by its worst moments, and that pleasure, when it arrives, is given the attention it needs to be remembered.
items.question: According to the passage, why does pleasure fade even when the things that gave it have not changed?

items.explanation: The passage says memory remembers the peak and forgets the rain, so a holiday is judged against the best remembered holiday, not against its own experience. That makes present moments seem inferior. The other options reverse the claim or invent a role for forgetting that the passage does not give.
options: Memory records every moment of a holiday with perfect accuracy
Memory makes every holiday seem better than it actually was at the time
Memory stores only the boring parts of an experience and discards the exciting parts
Memory prevents all comparison between different experiences
Memory selectively recalls the peak of a past experience, so the present is judged against an unusually high standard and found wanting
items.question: What role does memory play in hedonic adaptation, according to the passage?

items.explanation: The author recommends varying routine, paying close attention to ordinary experiences, and refusing to let a remembered peak become the standard. Acquiring more, seeking only novelty at any cost, and remembering only peaks all contradict that advice, and the passage says noticing is a practised skill, not a permanent cure.
options: Acquiring more of the things that pleased us in the past, in larger quantities
Seeking only extreme novelty and avoiding all familiar experiences
Varying the routine, attending closely to ordinary experiences, and refusing to let a remembered peak set the standard
Remembering only the peaks of past experiences so the present is constantly challenged
Accepting that noticing is impossible and that pleasure cannot be practised
items.question: What does the author propose for sustaining pleasure?

items.explanation: The passage argues a lecture sold by the hour can be tailored to the buyer but not to the discipline, and it stops being an invitation to think when the student treats it as a product to consume. A degree does not lose all value, teaching is not identical to shoemaking in the relevant sense, and the author does not say money has no place.
options: Education becomes more valuable when it is sold by the hour like any other service
A degree loses all value the moment a student pays tuition for it
Teaching is exactly the same as shoemaking, since both produce a finished object
Treating knowledge as a product changes the relationship, because the student becomes a customer entitled to satisfaction rather than a learner required to struggle
Money has no place in education and all universities should be free
items.passage: When knowledge is bought and sold, something changes in the relationship between teacher and student. A shoemaker sells a shoe; the customer judges it by whether it fits. A teacher sells, or is paid to provide, an understanding; but understanding cannot be handed over like a shoe. It must be built by the learner, often slowly and with difficulty. The moment knowledge is treated as a product, the student becomes a customer, and the customer is always right. A difficult idea is then experienced not as a challenge to be met but as a defect in the product, and the teacher who insists on difficulty is seen as providing poor service. This is not an argument against paying teachers. It is an argument about what payment can and cannot buy. Payment can buy time, attention and expertise, but it cannot buy the transformation that learning requires, because that transformation happens inside the learner. Universities that market themselves as providers of a student experience are therefore selling a promise they cannot keep. They can promise comfortable rooms and prompt replies, but they cannot promise that a student will emerge changed, since change depends on the student's own effort. The danger is that the language of the market quietly rewrites the purpose of education. Courses are judged by satisfaction scores, departments by enrolment numbers, and ideas by their marketability. The difficult, the unfashionable and the slow are squeezed out, not because they are worthless but because they do not sell. Knowledge, in this account, is not a product to be consumed but a practice to be entered into, and a university that forgets the difference may keep its customers happy while failing its students entirely. Online courses make the tension sharper, because they can be bought, paused and replayed like any other product, and their marketing promises transformation in a fixed number of hours. A learner who buys such a course may feel entitled to the outcome, and may blame the course when the outcome does not arrive, forgetting that the course can only provide material, not the effort that turns material into understanding. The best online teachers know this, and they design for effort, setting tasks that cannot be completed by watching alone, and building communities in which learners must explain ideas to each other. That design is harder to sell than a promise of effortless learning, but it is honest about what education is, and learners who accept the bargain often learn more than those who were promised a shortcut.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about treating knowledge as a product?

items.explanation: The passage says payment can buy time, attention and expertise but cannot buy the transformation learning requires, because that happens inside the learner. It does not say teachers should be unpaid, that satisfaction scores are sufficient, or that students need no effort.
options: Payment can buy time, attention and expertise, but it cannot buy the inner transformation that learning requires
Paying teachers is itself the cause of all problems in universities
Satisfaction scores are the only reliable measure of whether learning has occurred
A university can guarantee that a paying student will emerge changed
Students need make no effort at all if they have paid for a course
items.question: According to the author, what can payment buy in education, and what can it not buy?

items.explanation: The passage says courses are judged by satisfaction, departments by enrolment and ideas by marketability, so difficult, unfashionable and slow subjects are squeezed out because they do not sell, not because they are worthless. The other options claim the opposite or invent a defence of marketability.
options: Difficult subjects are squeezed out because they are worthless
Difficult, unfashionable and slow subjects are squeezed out because they do not sell well, even though they may be valuable
Marketability is the best test of whether an idea is true
Satisfaction scores prove that students have learned deeply
Enrolment numbers are irrelevant to how a university is run
items.question: Why, according to the passage, do difficult and unfashionable subjects disappear under market language?

items.explanation: The passage says work can feel meaningless when the worker cannot see the purpose, the task is fragmented, and the reward is unrelated to the value created, and that meaning is made through connection and craft. Higher pay alone, larger companies and more leisure are not presented as the cure.
options: Work is meaningless whenever it is paid, because payment corrupts all labour
Work is meaningless only when it is performed by machines rather than by people
Work feels meaningless when the worker cannot see its purpose, when the task is fragmented, and when the reward is unrelated to the value created
Work is meaningful whenever it is performed in a large company with many employees
Work is meaningless only for people who have no leisure time outside work
items.passage: Capitalism is remarkably good at producing jobs and remarkably bad at explaining why they matter. A worker may spend a career moving numbers between spreadsheets, attending meetings about meetings, and producing reports that no one reads, while being told that the work is vital. The pay may be good, the office may be pleasant, and still the worker may feel that the job is, in a real sense, pointless. This feeling is not laziness. It is a response to a structure in which the connection between effort and outcome has been broken. Three features make work feel meaningless. The first is distance from purpose: the worker cannot see who benefits from the work or how. The second is fragmentation: the task is so small a slice of a larger process that its contribution is invisible. The third is a mismatch between reward and value: the worker is paid for presence, not for the usefulness of what is produced. Meaning, when it appears, comes from the opposite conditions: a clear line from effort to a human outcome, a task whole enough to be owned, and a reward that tracks the value created rather than the hours endured. None of this means every job must be heroic. A bus driver, a nurse and a cleaner all do work whose purpose is visible, and that visibility is part of why such jobs, however modestly paid, are often described as meaningful. The question for an economy is therefore not only how many jobs it creates, but what kind of jobs, and whether the people who hold them can see, in their daily work, a reason for doing it that survives the end of the working day. Gig work sharpens the problem, because a driver or delivery worker may be paid per task, rated by customers and managed by an algorithm, without ever seeing the person who benefits from the work or understanding how the rating is calculated. The work is visible in the sense that it is constantly measured, yet invisible in the sense that its purpose is hidden behind a screen. Workers in such jobs often describe a strange combination of exhaustion and emptiness, of being busy all day and feeling that nothing has been accomplished. The remedy, if there is one, is not to romanticise the past, when many jobs were also tedious, but to ask, for each new form of work, whether the worker can see the outcome, own a part of the task, and be rewarded for value rather than for mere availability.
items.question: According to the passage, when does work feel meaningless?

items.explanation: The passage gives bus driver, nurse and cleaner as examples of modestly paid work whose purpose is visible, and says that visibility is part of why such jobs are described as meaningful. It does not claim pay determines meaning, that all jobs must be heroic, or that only professional work matters.
options: Modestly paid work can be meaningful when its purpose is visible to the worker, as with a bus driver, a nurse or a cleaner
Only heroic or highly paid work can ever be meaningful
Meaning in work is determined entirely by salary, so low pay always means low meaning
A job is meaningful only if it is performed in a large organisation
Visibility of purpose makes work less meaningful, because it creates pressure
items.question: The examples of the bus driver, the nurse and the cleaner are used to show that

items.explanation: The author says the question for an economy is not only how many jobs it creates but what kind, and whether holders can see a reason for doing it that survives the working day. Counting jobs alone, maximising pay, and ignoring purpose all contradict that conclusion.
options: An economy should be judged only by the number of jobs it creates
An economy should maximise pay regardless of the kind of work performed
An economy should ignore whether workers understand the purpose of their jobs
An economy should be judged by the kind of jobs it creates and whether workers can see a reason for their work beyond the working day
An economy should ensure that no job is ever fragmented or specialised
items.question: Which conclusion does the author draw about how an economy should be judged?

items.explanation: The passage says exile is not only physical departure but a condition of being between languages and customs, where home is remembered more sharply and the new place never fully accepts the exile. It is not about forgetting, wealth, or a purely voluntary choice.
options: Exile is a purely physical condition that ends as soon as a person crosses a border
Exile is a condition of being between languages, customs and loyalties, where home is remembered more sharply and the new place never fully accepts the exile
Exile always makes a person forget the country they left behind
Exile is experienced only by wealthy people who travel for pleasure
Exile is a voluntary choice that carries no loss or grief
items.passage: Exile is usually imagined as a physical condition: a person leaves one country and lives in another. Yet the writers who have lived it describe something subtler, a condition of being between languages, between customs, between loyalties, fully at home in neither place. The exile remembers the home country more sharply than those who stayed, because memory, freed from daily routine, preserves what was loved and discards what was resented. At the same time, the new country never quite accepts the exile, however fluent the language or long the residence, because belonging is not only a matter of papers or pronunciation. It is a matter of shared jokes, unspoken references and a history that cannot be acquired in a single lifetime. The result is a double vision. The exile sees both societies more clearly than those who have only ever lived in one, noticing assumptions that natives take for granted. That clarity is a gift, but it is also a wound, because seeing clearly does not mean belonging fully. Some exiles respond by building a portable home, carrying recipes, songs and rituals from place to place, so that home becomes something carried rather than somewhere lived. Others respond by refusing all homes, treating rootlessness as a kind of freedom. Both strategies are attempts to answer the same question: how does a person live well when the place that made them is no longer the place where they live? The answer, if there is one, is not return, which is rarely possible, but a way of holding two places at once without demanding that either one be enough. The children of exiles inherit a different version of the condition, growing up in a country their parents left, speaking a language their parents speak imperfectly, and feeling foreign in both the home of their parents and the home of their birth. They may be asked where they are really from, a question that assumes a single answer, and they may struggle to give one, because their answer is plural. Some embrace that plurality, treating it as a resource, a capacity to move between worlds that others cannot. Others experience it as a burden, a sense of never being fully claimed by any place. Either way, their experience shows that exile is not a single generation's story, but a condition that echoes, reshaping identity long after the original departure has become history.
items.question: According to the passage, what is the deeper nature of exile?

items.explanation: The passage says the exile sees both societies more clearly than those who lived in only one, noticing assumptions natives take for granted, and calls that clarity a gift and a wound because seeing clearly does not mean belonging fully. It does not claim exiles belong everywhere or forget either place.
options: Exiles belong fully in both countries at once
Exiles forget both countries and live entirely in the present
Exiles are unable to see any society clearly because they are confused
Exiles belong fully in the new country once they learn its language
Exiles see both societies more clearly than those who lived in only one, but that clarity does not bring full belonging
items.question: What does the author mean by the exile's double vision?

items.explanation: The passage says some build a portable home carrying recipes, songs and rituals, while others refuse all homes and treat rootlessness as freedom, both answering how to live well when home is elsewhere. Return is described as rarely possible, and neither strategy is said to erase loss.
options: Some build a portable home from recipes, songs and rituals, while others refuse all homes and treat rootlessness as freedom
All exiles return to their home country as soon as they are able to do so
All exiles forget their home country completely and adopt the new one without reserve
Exiles never attempt to answer the question of how to live well away from home
Both strategies erase the loss of exile entirely
items.question: According to the passage, how do exiles respond to living away from the place that made them?

items.explanation: The passage says an AI decision can be correct in outcome yet unjust in process if no one can explain it, and that a judge who cannot give reasons is not trusted even when right. Accuracy alone, speed, and cost are not presented as sufficient for legitimacy.
options: An AI system is legitimate whenever it is faster than a human judge
An AI system is legitimate whenever it is cheaper to run than a human process
An AI system is legitimate whenever its predictions are accurate, regardless of whether anyone can explain them
An AI decision can be correct in outcome yet unjust in process if no one can explain or challenge how it was reached
An AI system is legitimate whenever it was trained on a large amount of data
items.passage: Artificial intelligence promises decisions that are faster, more consistent and less biased than human judgement. A loan application can be scored in seconds, a resume can be screened without fatigue, a medical scan can be read without distraction. The promise is real, and so is the problem it hides. A decision can be correct in its outcome and still be unjust in its process, if no one can explain how it was reached or challenge it when it is wrong. A human judge who refuses to give reasons is not trusted, even when the verdict is right, and an algorithm should be held to no lower standard. The difficulty is that modern AI systems are often opaque by design. They learn patterns from data that no human fully understands, and their internal reasoning cannot be translated into the kind of explanation a person can accept or contest. This creates a new kind of power: decisions that affect lives, made by systems that cannot be questioned in the language of reasons. The remedy is not to abandon AI, but to insist that certain decisions require explanation as a condition of legitimacy. Where a decision cannot be explained, it should not be the final word; a human must be able to review it, override it, and take responsibility for it. Transparency is often proposed as the answer, but transparency of code is not the same as intelligibility of reasons. Publishing a million lines of code tells a rejected applicant nothing about why she was rejected. What matters is not that the system can be inspected, but that its decision can be justified to the person it affects, in terms she can understand and, if necessary, dispute. Hiring is one of the places where this matters most, because a rejected applicant is rarely told why, and the reasons, when they exist, are often buried in a model that no recruiter can explain. A candidate who is told only that she did not meet the criteria cannot know whether the criteria were fair, whether her application was read at all, or whether a different presentation would have changed the outcome. She cannot improve, she cannot appeal, and she cannot trust the process, even if the process was, in outcome, correct. A hiring system that can explain itself, even briefly, in terms a candidate can understand, does more than satisfy curiosity. It preserves the legitimacy of the institution, and it gives the candidate a reason to try again, rather than a reason to conclude that the system is arbitrary.
items.question: What is the author's central argument about AI decisions?
items.set_title: RC5: AI Ethics and Explainable Decisions

items.explanation: The passage says transparency of code is not the same as intelligibility of reasons, and publishing a million lines tells a rejected applicant nothing about why she was rejected. What matters is justification in terms she can understand and dispute, not code inspection alone.
options: Publishing code is sufficient, because anyone can read a million lines of code
Transparency of code is not the same as intelligibility of reasons; a decision must be justifiable to the affected person in terms she can understand and dispute
AI systems should never be inspected by anyone outside the company that built them
Rejected applicants do not need to know why they were rejected
Code transparency automatically produces an explanation a person can contest
items.question: Why does the author distinguish transparency of code from intelligibility of reasons?
items.set_title: RC5: AI Ethics and Explainable Decisions

items.explanation: The author says where a decision cannot be explained it should not be the final word, and a human must review, override and take responsibility for it. Abandoning AI, accepting opaque decisions as final, and hiding the system all contradict that remedy.
options: AI should be abandoned entirely in all decisions that affect people
Opaque AI decisions should be accepted as final, because human review would slow them down
Where a decision cannot be explained, it should not be the final word; a human must be able to review it, override it and take responsibility for it
AI systems should be hidden from the people they affect so they cannot be questioned
Human review is unnecessary because AI systems are always more consistent than humans
items.question: What remedy does the author propose for opaque AI decisions?
items.set_title: RC5: AI Ethics and Explainable Decisions

items.explanation: The poem lists her keeping ration cards, a broken clock, children's drawings and the smell of rain, and says a life can be packed into a suitcase yet still not fit, which is a metaphor for memory and identity surviving displacement. The other readings ignore the listed objects or invent a literal complaint about luggage.
options: The mother is a careless traveller who packs the wrong things
The mother is trying to impress the neighbours with her possessions
The mother has forgotten how to speak the language of her new home
The mother is angry at the children for drawing on the walls
The mother carries small, ordinary objects as a portable home, showing that identity and memory can survive displacement even when a place is lost
items.passage: My mother packed the monsoon in a suitcase, / a ration card, a clock that had stopped at four, / the smell of rain on a tin roof in July, / and three drawings my brother made of a house / with a door too small for anyone to enter. // She unpacked them in a city where the rain fell politely, / where no one asked about the village, / and the neighbours smiled at the sound of her name / as if it were a word they had not learned to say. // At night she wound the broken clock, / as if time, too, could be coaxed back, / and of a home that was still home, even after it was gone. // A life, she said, can be packed into a suitcase, / and still not fit, and still be carried, / in the small, exact weight of what we choose to keep.
items.question: What does the mother's packing chiefly suggest in the poem?

items.explanation: Winding a broken clock is a futile but tender act of trying to restore lost time, matching the stories of a river changing course and a train that never came. It is not a practical repair, a hobby, or a sign she believes the clock works.
options: She believes the clock is still working and keeps accurate time
She is performing a futile, tender act of trying to coax lost time back, as with the stories of what has changed or never arrived
She is repairing the clock so it can be sold for money
She winds the clock every night as a hobby with no emotional meaning
She is trying to wake the children by making a loud noise
items.question: The image of winding the broken clock most nearly suggests that

items.explanation: The argument assumes people who own dogs are healthier for other reasons, or that dog ownership itself causes the health, so it must assume no third factor explains both. The other options are stronger claims the argument does not need, such as every owner being healthier or dogs being the only cause.
options: People who own dogs are healthier because of dog ownership itself, rather than because of other differences between owners and non-owners
Every person who owns a dog is healthier than every person who does not
Dogs are the only cause of good health in any population
People who do not own dogs never exercise at all
Dog ownership is more important than diet, sleep and medical care combined
items.question: A survey finds that people who own dogs are healthier on average than people who do not. A writer concludes that owning a dog improves health. Which assumption is required?

items.explanation: If the new manager also introduced a training programme at the same time, the training is an alternative cause for the fall in errors, weakening the claim that the policy alone caused it. Staff liking the policy, the manager's experience, and errors falling in another department are weaker or irrelevant.
options: Some staff said they liked the new checking policy
The new manager had ten years of experience in quality control
The new manager also introduced a training programme for all staff at the same time as the checking policy
Errors also fell slightly in a department that did not adopt the policy
The checking policy was popular with senior staff in particular
items.question: A factory introduces a new checking policy under a new manager, and errors fall by 30 percent in three months. The manager argues the policy caused the fall. Which finding most weakens the argument?

items.explanation: Because the two groups differ in sleep and study time as well as in music listening, those differences could explain the memory difference, so the study cannot establish that music alone caused it. It does not prove music harms memory, nor that music has no effect.
options: Listening to classical music while studying always improves memory
Classical music has no effect on memory at all
Students who do not listen to classical music will always have worse memory
The study cannot establish that classical music alone caused the difference, because the groups also differed in sleep and study time
Sleep and study time are irrelevant to memory
items.question: A study finds students who listen to classical music while studying score better on memory tests than students who do not. However, the music listeners also sleep more and study for longer. Which conclusion is best supported?

items.explanation: Incorrigible means incapable of being corrected or reformed, so unreformable is closest. Corrigible is its opposite, corruptible concerns bribery, correctable is the opposite sense, and incredible means unbelievable rather than unreformable.
options: Corruptible
Unreformable
Correctable
Incredible
Corrigible
items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to INCORRIGIBLE.

items.explanation: Neither nor takes the nearer subject, the committee, which is singular in this collective sense, so has is correct, while the other options mismatch singular and plural subjects and verbs. The number takes has, each takes is, and the team along with the coach takes is, not are.
options: Neither the chairman nor the committee members was present.
Each of the proposals are under review.
Neither the chairman nor the committee members have been informed.
The number of errors are increasing every week.
Neither the chairman nor the committee has been informed.
items.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

items.explanation: The order must open with the old library, then its silence, then the librarian's fear, then the return of readers, then the lesson, giving C, A, D, B, E. Starting with E states the lesson before the story, and B before D returns readers before the librarian's decision.
options: C, A, D, B, E
A, C, D, B, E
C, D, A, B, E
E, C, A, D, B
B, C, A, D, E
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The shelves stood full and silent, and the librarian wondered if anyone would ever return. (B) Within a year, the reading room was full again, not because the books had changed but because the door had been opened. (C) The old library on the hill had survived fire, flood and a change of government. (D) She began to leave the door open at dawn, to put a chair outside, and to greet every passer-by by name. (E) A library, she learned, is not a storehouse of books but a habit of welcome. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sequence runs from the town's complaint, to the mayor's promise, to the bridge opening, to the empty road, to the lesson that a road needs a destination, giving A, C, B, D, E. Opening with E states the lesson first, and B before C opens the bridge before it is promised.
options: A, B, C, D, E
E, A, C, B, D
A, C, B, D, E
C, A, B, E, D
B, A, C, D, E
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The town had complained for years that it was cut off from the market. (B) The bridge opened with speeches, flags and a brass band. (C) The mayor promised a bridge, and the promise won him the election. (D) A year later, the bridge stood empty, because no road led from it to the market. (E) A bridge, the town learned, is useless without a road to somewhere. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sentence needs a word meaning long lasting and a word meaning brief: perennial for the dispute and ephemeral for the attention fits, while transient and enduring reverse the required senses. The other pairs mix a long word with a permanent word or a short word with a long word in the wrong places.
options: transient and enduring
ephemeral and perennial
perennial and transient
perennial and ephemeral
enduring and ephemeral
items.question: Fill in the blanks with the most appropriate pair. The border dispute is _______, having survived three generations of negotiations, while the media attention it attracts is _______, lasting barely a week. (1) perennial (2) ephemeral (3) transient (4) enduring

items.explanation: A man reading a book labelled History while the queue passes him shows that people rush toward a future they have not understood, ignoring the past that could guide them. The literal readings miss the labels, and the queue being efficient or the book being heavy are not the point.
options: Reading history is a waste of time when a queue is moving quickly
People should always join the longest queue available
The man is blocking the queue and should move aside
History books are too heavy to carry in a queue
People rush toward a future they have not understood, ignoring the lessons of the past that could guide them
items.question: The cartoon shows a long queue of people hurrying toward a door labelled The Future, while one man sits to the side calmly reading a thick book labelled History. The people in the queue do not look at him or at the book. What message does the cartoon most likely convey?

items.explanation: If patients rank proven safety records over price, MedCore's safety history is a genuine advantage that a price war would waste, while matching the generic price destroys the margin that funds that safety work. A rival price rise later and a possible new drug do not change the current choice. Cheaper distribution alone does not justify cutting the drug price. A smaller pack is a tactic, not a reason to hold price.
options: The generic maker plans to raise its price after six months
A recent survey shows that most patients and doctors rank a proven safety record above a lower price when choosing a diabetes medicine
MedCore may launch a new diabetes drug in three years
MedCore has found a cheaper way to distribute its drug to pharmacies
MedCore could launch a smaller pack at a lower price per pack
items.passage: MedCore is a mid-sized Indian pharmaceutical firm whose best-selling diabetes tablet, used by four lakh patients, has just lost patent protection. Within two months, three generic makers have launched the same molecule at 40 percent below the MedCore price, and MedCore has already lost 25 percent of its prescriptions. The generic firms spend almost nothing on medical education or safety monitoring, while MedCore runs a patient support programme, funds a pharmacovigilance team that tracks side effects, and maintains a cold chain that smaller firms skip. The marketing head wants to cut the MedCore price by 35 percent to match the generics, arguing that price is now the only difference patients see and that volume will recover. The medical affairs head warns that a 35 percent cut would force the closure of the pharmacovigilance team and the patient support programme, which are the reasons doctors trust the brand. The finance head notes that the drug contributes 45 percent of company revenue, and that a price cut of that size would push the whole firm into a loss, while holding price would lose market share more slowly. A survey of 1,500 doctors shows that 55 percent prescribe mainly on price, 30 percent on trust and safety history, and 15 percent on patient demand. The firm must decide before the next quarterly tender for hospital supplies, because the tender locks prices for six months and a wrong price cannot be changed mid-contract. The hospital tender covers 200 hospitals and the price agreed will apply for six months, so a wrong price cannot be corrected until the next tender round. The pharmacovigilance team has 12 staff and costs 2 crore rupees a year to run. The patient support programme sends reminders to 50,000 patients and has been praised by doctors in two published surveys. The generic makers have no such programmes and spend almost nothing on safety monitoring.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support holding the MedCore price instead of matching the generic price?

items.explanation: Keeping the current price while funding doctor education and safety support protects the trust advantage that differentiates MedCore, and it avoids the loss-making cut. Cutting price to match destroys the margin that pays for safety work. Raising the price in response to a cheaper rival is incoherent. Withdrawing from hospitals gives up the largest channel. Copying the generic model abandons the very services doctors value.
options: Cut the price by 35 percent immediately and close the patient support programme
Raise the price by 10 percent to signal premium quality
Hold the current price, invest the margin in doctor education about safety monitoring and in a visible quality guarantee, and compete on trust rather than price
Withdraw from hospital tenders and sell only through small pharmacies
Stop the pharmacovigilance team and copy the generic makers' low-cost model
items.question: What should MedCore do before the hospital tender?

items.explanation: If doctors already trust MedCore and would stay at a modest discount, the case for a deep 35 percent cut collapses, since a small discount protects share without destroying margin. A rival offering to partner is a different issue. Patients switching for small savings supports cutting, not holding. Rising raw material costs argue against any cut. A future drug does not affect this decision.
options: The generic makers have offered to partner with MedCore on distribution
Patients say they switch brands for even a small saving
Raw material costs for the drug are rising sharply
Doctors say they would keep prescribing MedCore if it offered only a 10 percent discount and a clear safety guarantee
MedCore plans to launch a new drug in three years
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the marketing head's argument for a 35 percent price cut?

items.explanation: If the river feeds drinking water for three villages, the pollution is a direct public health harm that outweighs any short-term profit, making the case for immediate action decisive. The effluent meeting an old standard does not change the real harm. A rival closing is irrelevant. A new filter technology arriving later does not justify delay. Low rainfall explains concentration but does not excuse the discharge.
options: The effluent meets the standard written 20 years ago
A rival factory in the same district closed last year
A cheaper filter technology will be available in two years
Low rainfall this year has reduced the river flow
The river downstream supplies drinking water to three villages and their cattle
items.passage: A paper mill on a river in central India has been discharging untreated effluent for six months after its treatment plant broke down. The mill employs 600 workers and is the largest employer in the district, and it contributes a large share of the local tax revenue. A local health worker has reported skin rashes and stomach illness among families who use river water, and a small study by a college found fish deaths downstream of the mill. The mill owner argues that repairing the treatment plant will cost 8 crore rupees, which the mill cannot afford after a bad year, and that closing the mill even temporarily would leave 600 families without income. The plant manager suggests diluting the effluent with more river water at night, which would reduce the visible colour but not the toxic load. The district officer has the power to order a closure but fears the political fallout of 600 lost jobs in an election year. The mill has been given a notice to fix the plant within 30 days, and the owner is lobbying for an extension of six months, promising to fix the plant when the next season's profits arrive. Meanwhile, the health complaints are rising, and the college study has been shared with a local newspaper. The health worker who reported the illness has kept a record of 40 families with skin rashes and stomach problems in the last three months. The college study tested water at five points along the river and found fish deaths at three of them. The district officer is facing an election in six months and has received petitions from both the mill workers and the village families. The mill's treatment plant was built 15 years ago and has broken down twice before, each time taking two months to repair.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support ordering an immediate halt to the discharge?
items.set_title: DM2: The River and the Mill

items.explanation: If the river water is the only source for the affected families, they cannot avoid the harm by switching sources, so the cost of delay falls entirely on people with no alternative. A small fine makes delay cheap and therefore weakens the case. A future repair promise does not protect people now. The mill paying for a health camp does not stop the exposure. Seasonal rain would dilute the effluent only temporarily.
options: The affected families have no alternative water source and depend entirely on the river
The fine for continued discharge is only 50,000 rupees per month
The mill owner has promised to repair the plant in six months
The mill has offered to fund a health camp for affected families
Rain in the next season is expected to dilute the effluent
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support refusing the six-month extension?
items.set_title: DM2: The River and the Mill

items.explanation: Promising to fix the plant when profits arrive is a pledge about future intent, not a fact showing the harm is small or avoidable, so it is not a reason to grant an extension. The health risk, the lack of alternative water, the legal notice, and the fact that dilution does not reduce toxicity are all genuine reasons to refuse.
options: Continued discharge is causing rising health complaints among river users
The owner has promised to fix the plant when the next season's profits arrive
The affected families have no alternative water source
Diluting the effluent at night does not reduce its toxic load
The district officer has already issued a formal notice requiring repair within 30 days
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to refuse the mill's request for a six-month extension EXCEPT
items.set_title: DM2: The River and the Mill

items.explanation: If other auditors have missed fraud after signing early, early sign-off is a known risk, not a safe favour, and the junior auditor has a concrete reason to refuse. The mentor being near retirement and the client being important do not change the fraud facts. A clean record in the past does not guarantee the current numbers are true. Promising to disclose later does not cure a false signature now.
options: The mentor is retiring in three months and wants a smooth final year
The client is the firm's largest source of revenue this year
A junior colleague in another firm was suspended after signing off early on a client whose fraud was found later
The mentor has never had a complaint in 25 years of practice
The mentor promises to disclose the gap to the client next quarter
items.passage: A junior auditor in a mid-sized firm has found that a client, a listed company, overstated its revenue by 12 percent in the last quarter through invoices issued before goods were delivered. The finding is documented and clear, but the engagement partner, who mentored the junior auditor for five years and helped the auditor get the job, wants the auditor to sign off on the accounts without mentioning the issue. The partner argues that the client will correct the invoices next quarter, that a qualified report would destroy the client's share price and cost the audit firm its largest client, and that the junior auditor owes the partner loyalty for past support. The junior auditor knows that signing a clean report would breach professional standards and could lead to suspension if the fraud is discovered, and that the regulator has recently punished two auditors for similar sign-offs. The auditor also knows that refusing will damage the relationship with the mentor and may affect the next appraisal. The report must be filed in five days, and the client has already told investors that results will be strong. The regulator has recently suspended two auditors from other firms for signing clean reports where revenue was overstated, and both cases were reported in the press. The audit firm has a quality review partner who is supposed to check all listed-company reports before they are filed, but the partner has not yet seen this report. The junior auditor joined the firm three years ago after a training contract and is due for promotion this year. The client has told investors that results will be strong and its share price rose after that announcement.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support refusing to sign the clean report?
items.set_title: DM3: The Auditor and the Mentor

items.explanation: Refusing to sign and documenting the finding through the firm's ethics channel protects the public, creates a record, and gives the firm a chance to correct the report before filing. Signing now and hoping for a later correction is a false statement. Resigning silently leaves the fraud unchallenged. Telling the client alone does not protect the auditor. Asking the mentor to sign instead shifts the signature without fixing the report.
options: Sign the clean report and hope the client corrects the invoices next quarter
Resign quietly without telling anyone about the finding
Tell the client informally but sign the report anyway
Refuse to sign, document the finding in writing, and escalate it through the firm's ethics and quality review channel before the filing deadline
Ask the mentor to sign the report instead of signing it personally
items.question: What should the junior auditor do?
items.set_title: DM3: The Auditor and the Mentor

items.explanation: If the inflated revenue was found in the same way last year and was corrected, the partner's promise of correction is a pattern of using next quarter as cover, not a credible assurance. A strong share price and a new auditor would not justify the sign-off. A written note from the partner is still a false report. The client having many employees is a reason the fraud matters more, not less.
options: The client's share price rose sharply after the last results announcement
The client has hired a new chief financial officer this year
The mentor has offered to give the auditor a written note taking full responsibility
The client employs 5,000 people across three states
The same revenue inflation was found last year and was also promised to be corrected next quarter
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the partner's argument that the client will correct the invoices next quarter?
items.set_title: DM3: The Auditor and the Mentor

items.explanation: If the best trainees leave because feedback arrives too late, slow feedback is a direct cause of attrition, which is the problem the firm is trying to solve. Office attendance being popular is a separate preference. A rival paying more explains some exits but not the feedback link. Mentors being busy is the cause of the delay, not a reason to accept it. Trainees wanting faster promotion is a different complaint.
options: Exit interviews show that the best trainees leave because they receive no feedback on their work for months
Trainees say they prefer working from the office three days a week
A rival firm pays its trainees 20 percent more
Senior mentors say they are too busy with client work to give feedback
Trainees say they want faster promotion to the next level
items.passage: A consulting firm hires 60 trainees each year for a two-year programme. In the last two years, 25 of the 60 trainees have left before completing the programme, most of them in the first eight months, and the firm has spent heavily on recruitment and training for people who leave. Exit interviews mention three recurring complaints: trainees receive feedback only at the six-month review, they are given repetitive data-cleaning work for months without seeing a client, and they are not told how their work connects to the project outcome. The human resources head wants to introduce monthly feedback sessions, a rotation across three different project teams in the first year, and a mentor for each trainee. The project heads resist, arguing that monthly feedback takes time away from billable work, that rotations disrupt teams, and that trainees should prove themselves on basic work before getting interesting tasks. The managing partner must decide before the next intake of 60 trainees joins in two months, and the cost of the proposed changes is small compared with the cost of replacing 25 trainees a year. The firm spends 18 lakh rupees on recruiting and training each trainee, and replacing 25 trainees a year costs far more than the proposed changes. The trainees who leave most often join rival firms that offer structured mentoring and earlier client work. The project heads are judged on billable hours, so time spent on feedback reduces their measured performance. The next intake of 60 trainees joins in two months, and the human resources head has warned that the same pattern will repeat unless the programme changes before they arrive.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support introducing monthly feedback sessions?

items.explanation: A structured rotation with a clear handover and a mentor addresses the complaint about repetitive work while limiting disruption, and it gives trainees a view of outcomes. Doing nothing keeps the attrition. A pay rise alone does not fix feedback or meaningful work. Banning resignations is unenforceable and would worsen morale. Longer probation increases the period of the very experience trainees are leaving.
options: Keep the current programme unchanged and hope the next intake is more patient
Introduce a structured rotation across three teams in the first year, with a clear handover for each move and a named mentor for every trainee
Raise trainee pay by 15 percent and change nothing else
Require trainees to sign a bond that prevents them leaving for two years
Extend the probation period from three months to nine months
items.question: What is the best response to the trainee attrition problem?

items.explanation: If trainees who get early client exposure stay far longer, the project heads' claim that trainees must prove themselves on basic work first is contradicted by the firm's own data. A rival offering rotations is a competitive pressure but not proof. Mentors being popular does not show early exposure works. Client confidentiality is a constraint to manage, not evidence against exposure. Trainee demand for faster promotion is a separate issue.
options: A rival firm offers rotations to all its trainees
Mentors are popular with trainees who have them
Trainees who were given early client exposure in a pilot stayed 18 months on average, against 8 months for those who were not
Clients have asked for stricter confidentiality on projects
Trainees have asked for faster promotion
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the project heads' argument that trainees should prove themselves on basic work before getting interesting tasks?

items.explanation: If the same two people received the top rating in four straight years without a documented reason, the pattern itself is evidence of bias rather than merit, strengthening the case for an independent review. The manager being liked and the team growing are not evidence of fairness. The other manager changing her mind is a procedural fact, not proof of bias. The firm having a policy does not show it was followed.
options: The manager is well liked by the senior leadership team
The team has grown from 20 people to 35 people in two years
The firm has a written appraisal policy that requires documented evidence
The same two people received the top rating in four straight years without any documented reason that distinguishes them from their peers
The other manager has agreed to change her ratings to match
items.passage: A technology company runs an annual appraisal in which each team member is rated by their manager, and the top 10 percent receive a large bonus and faster promotion. This year, two managers who share a team of 40 people disagree sharply. One manager gave the top rating to two people who work closely with that manager on a flagship project, while the other manager, who supervises the same people on a second project, rated both of them as average, citing missed deadlines and errors that had to be fixed by others. The first manager argues that the flagship work is more visible and more valuable, and that the errors were minor. The second manager has produced emails showing the missed deadlines and the rework. The human resources head must decide whether to accept the first manager's ratings, accept the second manager's ratings, or order an independent review by a panel that includes neither manager. The two employees have already heard that they may receive the top rating and are expecting the bonus, while six other employees who met all their targets are watching the outcome closely and have said they will lose faith in the appraisal system if the top ratings go to people with documented errors. The bonus pool for the top 10 percent is fixed, so giving the top rating to one person means another person loses it. The six employees who met all their targets have worked on the same projects and have asked the human resources head how the ratings were decided. The first manager has been with the firm for eight years and is known for defending the flagship team, while the second manager joined two years ago from a rival firm. The appraisal results must be announced next week.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support ordering an independent review?

items.explanation: If the missed deadlines were caused by the first manager's own late instructions, the errors do not belong to the employees at all, which undermines the second manager's ratings and the first manager's defence equally, leaving an independent review as the only fair route. The flagship project being important supports the first manager. A bonus being large raises stakes but does not resolve the facts. The employees expecting a bonus is a consequence, not evidence. The panel being slow is a practical cost, not a reason to decide on contested facts.
options: The flagship project is the most important project in the company this year
The bonus attached to the top rating is worth six months of salary
The two employees are already expecting the bonus
An independent panel would take three weeks to complete its review
The missed deadlines were caused by the first manager giving instructions late, not by the employees' own delays
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the second manager's case for the average ratings?

items.explanation: Accepting the first manager's ratings without checking the emails would reward the very pattern the other employees are watching, so a fair process must weigh the evidence first. The other options all point to a review: the written policy requires evidence, the emails are evidence, the risk of losing faith is real, and the expectation of a bonus does not create an entitlement.
options: Accept the first manager's ratings without examining the second manager's evidence
The appraisal policy requires documented evidence for the top rating
The second manager has produced emails showing missed deadlines and rework
Six employees who met their targets say they will lose faith in the system if the ratings stand
The two employees are already expecting the bonus
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to order an independent review EXCEPT

items.explanation: If salaries are already visible through a leaked spreadsheet, secrecy has already failed and a transparent, published pay structure is the only way to restore trust. A policy against discussing pay does not undo the leak. The leaker resigning does not fix the pay gaps. The rival paying more is a separate issue. Junior staff being upset is the problem, not a reason for secrecy.
options: The firm has a strict policy against employees discussing pay
A leaked spreadsheet has already made most salaries visible to the whole office
The employee who leaked the data has offered to resign
A rival firm pays 15 percent more for the same roles
Junior staff are upset about the pay gaps they discovered
items.passage: A mid-sized marketing agency has a strict policy of pay confidentiality, and salaries are decided by the founder with no published bands. A junior employee has leaked a spreadsheet showing that two people doing the same job earn 40 percent apart, that a new hire earns more than a person with five years in the firm, and that one employee is paid far less than others of the same level. The leak has spread across the office in a day, and morale has fallen sharply. The founder wants to find the leaker and dismiss the person, arguing that the leak broke a clear rule and that confidentiality must be enforced. The human resources head argues that the real problem is the unexplained pay gaps, and that punishing the leaker without addressing the gaps will make the resentment worse. The finance head warns that fixing the gaps by raising the lower salaries would cost 12 lakh rupees a year, which the firm can afford only by delaying a planned office move. The founder must decide this week, because the annual salary review is due and employees are waiting to see whether the firm will act on the information in the spreadsheet. The annual salary review is due this week and employees are waiting to see whether the gaps will be corrected. The founder started the agency 12 years ago and has always decided pay personally, with no published bands or review process. The planned office move would cost 30 lakh rupees and was meant to give the growing team more space. The finance head has calculated that correcting the gaps would cost 12 lakh rupees a year, which the firm can afford only by delaying the move.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support publishing clear pay bands and fixing the unexplained gaps?

items.explanation: If the lower-paid employee has the same qualifications and a longer record, the gap cannot be explained by merit and is an unfairness the firm must correct rather than a market outcome to defend. A market shortage for the new hire is a possible justification. The founder deciding alone is the process that created the problem. A planned office move is a competing priority, not a justification. The leaker breaking a rule does not make the pay gap fair.
options: The new hire works in a skill that is in short supply in the market
Pay decisions are made by the founder alone with no review
The lower-paid employee has the same qualifications and a longer service record than the higher-paid colleague doing the same job
The firm has delayed its office move once before
The leaker broke a clear confidentiality rule
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support raising the lower salaries rather than defending the gaps?

items.explanation: Delaying the office move to fund a fair pay structure, while addressing the leak through a proper process, fixes the substantive problem and treats the breach separately. Dismissing the leaker alone leaves the gaps in place. Keeping pay secret after the leak is impossible. Raising only one salary leaves other gaps. Freezing all salaries punishes everyone for a problem the firm created.
options: Dismiss the leaker immediately and keep the pay structure secret
Raise only the lowest salary and ignore the other gaps
Freeze all salaries for a year
Delay the planned office move, publish pay bands, correct the unexplained gaps, and handle the leak through the firm's normal disciplinary process
Promise to review pay next year with no changes now
items.question: What should the founder do?

items.explanation: If the outage affected hospitals and emergency services, the failure is a public safety matter, not a commercial dispute, so a transparent admission and a funded backup plan are essential. The vendor offering a discount does not change the risk. The provider being the cheapest explains the choice but does not excuse it. Competitors suffering the same outage does not reduce this firm's duty. The contract lacking a penalty clause shows the contract was weak, not that no action is needed.
options: The vendor has offered a 20 percent discount on next year's fees
The vendor was the cheapest provider when the contract was signed
Rival firms using the same provider also suffered the outage
The contract has no penalty clause for downtime
The outage affected hospitals and emergency services that rely on the firm's software
items.passage: A software firm that sells appointment and billing systems to 300 clinics and hospitals moved its entire platform to a single cloud provider two years ago to save costs. Last week, the provider suffered a 14-hour outage, and the firm's customers could not access patient records, book appointments or issue bills. Two hospitals had to return to paper records, and one clinic reported that a patient waited six hours for a repeat prescription. The provider has apologised and offered a service credit worth one month of fees, but it has not explained the cause of the outage or what it will change. The firm's chief executive must decide whether to stay with the provider, move to a second provider for backup, or build an in-house system. Moving to a second provider would cost 40 lakh rupees a year, building in-house would cost 2 crore rupees and take a year, and staying costs nothing extra. The sales head argues that the outage was a one-off event and that customers have already forgiven the firm. The technology head argues that a single point of failure for hospital software is unacceptable, and that the firm cannot promise reliability it does not control. The firm must answer its customers this week, and its largest hospital customer has asked for a written plan. The largest hospital customer has asked for a written plan by Friday and has said it will review its contract if no plan arrives. The service credit offered by the provider is worth one month of fees, which is a small sum compared with the revenue the firm lost during the outage. Building an in-house system would take a year and cost 2 crore rupees, and the firm would need to hire five engineers it does not currently have.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support moving to a second provider for backup?

items.explanation: A published incident report, a funded backup provider and a written reliability plan give the hospital customer evidence rather than reassurance, and they address the single point of failure directly. Staying silent, blaming the vendor, or promising the impossible all leave the risk in place. A discount alone does not change reliability.
options: Publish an incident report, move to a second provider for backup, and give the hospital customer a written reliability plan with timelines
Say nothing and hope customers forget the outage
Blame the cloud provider publicly and take no further action
Promise customers that no outage will ever happen again
Accept the service credit and continue with the single provider
items.question: What should the chief executive tell the hospital customer this week?

items.explanation: The cost of a backup is a financial consideration in favour of staying, not a criticism of the plan to move, so it is the exception. The risk to patients, the lack of a cause or a fix from the provider, the absence of a penalty, and the duty to customers who cannot work without the system are all genuine criticisms of staying with a single provider.
options: The outage disrupted hospitals and emergency services
The provider has not explained the cause or what it will change
The contract has no penalty clause for downtime
A second provider would cost 40 lakh rupees a year
Customers cannot access patient records or issue bills during an outage
items.question: All of the following are valid criticisms of staying with the single cloud provider EXCEPT
A shopkeeper sells an article for Rs 1320 after allowing a 20% discount on its marked price, and still makes a profit of 10%. What is the cost price of the article?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 1320 / 0.80 = Rs 1650. The selling price of Rs 1320 is 10% above the cost price, so the cost price is Rs 1320 / 1.10 = Rs 1200. The marked price is a distractor here: working from it without removing the profit margin gives the wrong figure, and using the discount on the cost price also misleads.

items.question: A car travels 240 km from Pune to Mumbai at 60 km/h and returns over the same route at 40 km/h. What is the average speed of the car for the whole journey?
options: 50 km/h
45 km/h
52 km/h
48 km/h
items.explanation: The time taken is 240/60 + 240/40 = 4 + 6 = 10 hours for 480 km, so the average speed is 480/10 = 48 km/h. The simple mean of the two speeds, 50 km/h, is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed; the harmonic mean is the correct tool here.

items.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 3:5 and their sum is 64. What is the difference between the two numbers?
items.explanation: The numbers are 64 x 3/8 = 24 and 64 x 5/8 = 40. Their difference is 40 - 24 = 16. Simply subtracting the ratio terms, 2, or halving the sum gives the wrong options.

items.question: Five students score distinct marks out of 100, and their average score is 32. What is the maximum possible value of the largest mark?
items.explanation: The sum of all 5 values is 5 x 32 = 160. To make the largest value as big as possible, the other 4 values must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, so they are 1, 2, 3, 4, summing to 10. The largest value is therefore 160 - 10 = 150. Forgetting that the values must be distinct, or using the average itself as the maximum, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days, B and C together in 15 days, and A and C together in 20 days. In how many days can all three working together finish the job?
options: 12 days
15 days
10 days
24 days
8 days
items.explanation: Adding the three pair rates gives 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = 1/5 per day, which counts each worker twice. Halving gives the combined rate of all three, 1/10 per day, so the time is 10 days. Using any single pair rate, or forgetting to halve, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A point is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. What is the length of the tangent drawn from the point to the circle?
options: 12 cm
8 cm
18 cm
10 cm
15 cm
items.explanation: The radius to the point of contact, the tangent and the line to the centre form a right triangle. The tangent length is sqrt(13 squared - 5 squared) = sqrt(144) = 12 cm. Using the distance itself, or adding the squares, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius 13 cm. What is the area of the square?
options: 169 sq cm
676 sq cm
338 sq cm
260 sq cm
300 sq cm
items.explanation: The diagonal of the square is the diameter, 26 cm. If the side is s, then s squared + s squared = 26 squared, so s squared = 338 and the area is 2 x 13 squared = 338 sq cm. This is also the largest rectangle that fits in the circle, so no inscribed square can be bigger.

items.question: A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is its area?
options: 90 sq cm
72 sq cm
96 sq cm
78 sq cm
84 sq cm
items.explanation: The semi-perimeter is (13+14+15)/2 = 21 cm. By Heron's formula the area is sqrt(21 x 8 x 7 x 6) = sqrt(7056) = 84 sq cm. Multiplying two sides and halving, which only works for a right triangle, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is the radius of its circumcircle?
options: 7 cm
8 cm
9 cm
6.5 cm
items.explanation: The area is 84 sq cm by Heron's formula. The circumradius is abc/(4 x area) = (13 x 14 x 15)/(4 x 84) = 2730/336 = 65/8 cm. The inradius is 4 cm, which is a different value and appears among the distractors.

items.question: What is the volume of a sphere of radius 21 cm? (Use pi = 22/7)
options: 31000 cubic cm
42000 cubic cm
38808 cubic cm
35280 cubic cm
45000 cubic cm
items.explanation: The volume is (4/3) x pi x r cubed = (4/3) x (22/7) x 9261 = 38808 cubic cm. Using the surface-area formula, or cubing the diameter, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the remainder when 12345 is divided by 9?
items.explanation: A number leaves the same remainder on division by 9 as the sum of its digits. The digit sum of 12345 is 1+2+3+4+5 = 15, and 15 leaves remainder 6 on division by 9, so 12345 leaves remainder 6. The digit sum itself, or the remainder on division by 3, gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many trailing zeroes does 50! have?
items.explanation: Trailing zeroes come from factors of 10, counted by factors of 5. There are 10 multiples of 5 and 2 multiples of 25 up to 50, so the number of trailing zeroes is 10 + 2 = 12. Counting only the multiples of 5, or counting multiples of 10, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the smallest positive integer that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, by 4 and by 5?
items.explanation: Such a number is 2 more than a common multiple of 3, 4 and 5. The LCM is 60, so the smallest such number is 60 + 2 = 62. The LCM itself leaves remainder 0, and the next candidate is 122, which is larger.

items.question: What is the maximum value of k such that 2 raised to the power k divides 100!?
items.explanation: The exponent of 2 in 100! is 50 + 25 + 12 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 97. That is the largest k with 2 to the power k dividing 100!. Counting only the even numbers, or using the exponent of 5, gives the wrong options.

items.question: If x + 1/x = 5, what is the value of x squared + 1/x squared?
items.explanation: Squaring gives (x + 1/x) squared = x squared + 2 + 1/x squared, so x squared + 1/x squared = 5 squared - 2 = 23. Squaring the value directly, or forgetting to subtract 2, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the maximum value of -2x squared + 12x - 10, where x is a real number?
items.explanation: Completing the square gives -2x squared + 12x - 10 = -2(x - 3) squared + 8. The squared term is never negative, so the expression is at most 8, attained at x = 3. The constant term, or the value at x = 0, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A bag contains 5 red balls and 4 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both balls are red?
items.explanation: There are C(9,2) = 36 ways to draw two balls and C(5,2) = 10 ways to draw two red balls, so the probability is 10/36 = 5/18. Using the ratio of red balls to all balls, or drawing with replacement, gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many four-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, without repetition of any digit?
items.explanation: The thousands place can be filled in 6 ways, the hundreds in 5 ways, the tens in 4 ways and the units in 3 ways, giving 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 = 360 numbers. Allowing repetition would give 6 to the power 4, and using fewer digits gives the wrong options.

items.question: Is the integer n odd? Statement I: 3n is odd. Statement II: n + 2 is odd.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Either statement alone is sufficient.
Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.
items.explanation: If 3n is odd then n must be odd, so statement I alone settles the question. If n + 2 is odd then n must be odd as well, so statement II alone also settles it. Hence either statement alone is sufficient, and the combined option is wrong.

items.question: What is the total number of employees in the company in 2024?

diagram.caption: Number of employees by department, 2023 and 2024

options: 1030 employees
1120 employees
1080 employees
1050 employees
1150 employees
items.explanation: Adding the 2024 column gives 250 + 130 + 65 + 230 + 95 + 310 = 1080 employees. The 2023 total is 950, which is a distractor.

items.question: Which department recorded the highest percentage growth in employees from 2023 to 2024?
options: IT
Sales
Marketing
HR
Finance
items.explanation: The growth rates are Sales 13.64%, Marketing 18.18%, HR -7.14%, IT 21.05%, Finance 18.75% and Operations 10.71%, so IT grew fastest. The largest absolute increase is in IT, but the question asks for percentage growth.

items.question: What percentage of the company's 2024 employees work in the IT department?
items.explanation: The IT department has 230 of the 1080 employees in 2024, which is 230/1080 x 100 = 21.3%. Using the 2023 total, or the IT headcount as a share of another department, gives the wrong options.

items.question: If the total smartphone market in 2025 is Rs 8000 crore, what are the sales of Brand B?

diagram.caption: Market share (%) of five smartphone brands, 2025

options: Rs 1600 crore
Rs 2400 crore
Rs 2000 crore
Rs 1800 crore
Rs 2800 crore
items.explanation: Brand B holds 25% of the market, so its sales are 25% of Rs 8000 crore = Rs 2000 crore. The other brands' shares give the wrong options.

items.question: What is the combined market share of Brand A and Brand C?
items.explanation: Brand A has 30% and Brand C has 20%, so together they hold 30 + 20 = 50%. Adding any other pair of shares gives the wrong options.

items.question: By how much do the sales of the largest brand exceed those of the smallest brand?
options: Rs 1200 crore
Rs 1600 crore
Rs 2000 crore
Rs 800 crore
Rs 2400 crore
items.explanation: The largest brand has 30% and the smallest has 10%, a gap of 20 percentage points, which is 20% of Rs 8000 crore = Rs 1600 crore. The gap between the top two brands is much smaller and is a distractor.

items.question: What is the total NPA amount across the three branches?

diagram.caption: Loans disbursed and NPA rates of three bank branches
diagram.content: A bank has three branches. Branch X disbursed loans of Rs 500 crore with an NPA rate of 4%. Branch Y disbursed loans of Rs 500 crore with an NPA rate of 6%. Branch Z disbursed loans of Rs 1000 crore with an NPA rate of 5%.

options: Rs 80 crore
Rs 120 crore
Rs 90 crore
Rs 130 crore
Rs 100 crore
items.explanation: The NPA amounts are X: Rs 20 crore, Y: Rs 30 crore and Z: Rs 50 crore, totalling Rs 100 crore. Adding the NPA rates, or the loan amounts, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Which branch has the largest NPA amount?
options: Branch Z
Branch X
Branch Y
Branches X and Y
All three are equal
items.explanation: The NPA amounts are X: Rs 20 crore, Y: Rs 30 crore and Z: Rs 50 crore, so Branch Z has the largest NPA amount. Branch Y has the highest NPA rate, but Branch Z's larger loan book gives it the biggest NPA amount.

items.question: What is the overall NPA rate of the bank across all three branches?
items.explanation: The total NPA is Rs 100 crore on total loans of Rs 2000 crore, so the overall rate is 100/2000 x 100 = 5%. Averaging the three branch rates gives 5%, which is wrong because the branches have different loan sizes.

items.question: Who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2025?
options: Laszlo Krasznahorkai
Jon Fosse
Han Kang
Annie Ernaux
Abdulrazak Gurnah
items.explanation: Laszlo Krasznahorkai, the Hungarian novelist, won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Literature. Han Kang won in 2024, Jon Fosse in 2023, Annie Ernaux in 2022, and Abdulrazak Gurnah in 2021, so none of them is the 2025 laureate.

items.question: Who won the ICC Women's Cricket World Cup in 2025?
options: Australia
India
England
South Africa
New Zealand
items.explanation: India won the 2025 ICC Women's Cricket World Cup, beating South Africa in the final at Navi Mumbai in November 2025 for its first title. Australia, the defending champion, was eliminated in the semi-final, and England and New Zealand did not reach the final.

items.question: Which term was chosen as the Oxford Word of the Year for 2025?
options: Brain rot
Slop
Rage bait
Vibe coding
Goblin mode
items.explanation: Rage bait was chosen as the Oxford Word of the Year for 2025, defined as online content deliberately designed to provoke anger to drive engagement. Brain rot was the 2024 choice and goblin mode was the 2022 choice, while slop and vibe coding were other prominent 2025 terms that did not win the Oxford title.

items.question: Operation Sindoor, launched by India in May 2025, was a military response to which event?
options: The Pulwama attack of 2019
The Uri attack of 2016
The Pathankot attack of 2016
The Pahalgam terror attack of April 2025
The Mumbai attacks of 2008
items.explanation: Operation Sindoor was launched on 7 May 2025 in response to the Pahalgam terror attack of 22 April 2025, in which 26 tourists were killed in Jammu and Kashmir. The Pulwama, Uri, Pathankot and Mumbai attacks were earlier incidents that drew different responses.

items.question: In 2025, India overtook which country to become the world's fourth-largest economy?
options: Germany
United Kingdom
France
Canada
Japan
items.explanation: India overtook Japan in 2025 to become the world's fourth-largest economy, according to International Monetary Fund data. Germany remained third, the United Kingdom sixth, and France and Canada were smaller economies than Japan at the time.

items.question: Which team won its first Indian Premier League title in 2025?
options: Royal Challengers Bengaluru
Punjab Kings
Delhi Capitals
Lucknow Super Giants
Gujarat Titans
items.explanation: Royal Challengers Bengaluru won their first Indian Premier League title in 2025, beating Punjab Kings in the final in June 2025. Punjab Kings were the runners-up, Gujarat Titans had already won in 2022, and Delhi Capitals and Lucknow Super Giants have never won the title.
